**Radicular pain** is a type of neuropathic pain caused by irritation or inflammation of a spinal nerve root. In the lumbar spine, it often presents as low back or buttock pain that radiates down the leg. Patients often describe this pain as sudden, shooting, burning, electric, sharp, or stabbing.

Radicular pain is a high-yield clinical topic because it connects spinal anatomy, pain physiology, neurological examination, and imaging to determine an appropriate management plan for each patient. It is also commonly encountered across a variety of specialties including primary care, emergency medicine, neurology, orthopedics, neurosurgery, and, of course, pain medicine.

**Estimated time:** 60–75 minutes

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- [ ] Define radicular pain and distinguish it from radiculopathy
- [ ] Explain how disc herniation and degenerative narrowing can cause radicular pain
- [ ] Understand traversing versus exiting nerve root involvement
- [ ] Localize common clinical patterns to specific nerve root levels
- [ ] Identify red flags and know when investigations are useful
- [ ] Compare conservative, interventional, and surgical management options

## Case example

The following case will be used as a point of reference throughout this module:

A previously healthy 24-year-old man develops sudden right leg pain while deadlifting. He has difficulty identifying exactly where the pain began, but describes an "electric shock" traveling down the leg.

:::: {.learning-callout .learning-callout--think .module-learning-callout role="note" aria-labelledby="radicular-pain-introduction-callout-2"}

```{=html}
<header class="learning-callout-header">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M9 18h6m-5 3h4M8.5 14.5a6 6 0 1 1 7 0c-1 .7-1.5 1.5-1.5 2.5h-4c0-1-.5-1.8-1.5-2.5Z" /></svg>
  <h3 id="radicular-pain-introduction-callout-2">Pause and think</h3>
</header>
```

::: {.learning-callout-body}

Based on the information you have so far, what features from this case suggest **radicular pain**?

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

There are two key features that make us think about radicular pain: the pain radiates down the leg, and it has an electric quality. Other descriptors patients may use include sharp, stabbing, shooting, or burning.

Before continuing to the next section, try to think about what could cause this type of pain in an otherwise healthy young patient.

</details>

:::
